Ciprix shows the team's CAD in AdvantageScope with moving parts following the real mechanisms (RobotVisualizer and MechanismPoses, in ciprix-core). It works the same way in simulation, on the robot and in log replay, because the poses come from the subsystems' inputs. Create an advantagescope/ folder at the root of the robot project: advantagescope/ Robot_MyRobot/ config.json robot configuration (hand-written, versioned) model.glb the chassis and everything that doesn't move (exported from CAD) model_0.glb the intake (moving part 0) config.generated.json generated by the simulation, not versioned

Leave the robot assembly in the mechanisms' start position, the same one the code treats as zero angle or zero height. The assembly's origin should be the center of the chassis, on the ground. If it isn't, adjust position in config.json and add the same value to each zeroedPosition. Export the chassis without the moving parts as model.glb (binary glTF). Export each moving part as a separate file, model_0.glb, model_1.glb and so on, in the same position it's in on the assembly (don't move the origin). In Onshape, one way is to suppress the other parts before exporting. The official conversion guide is at Converting Onshape & STEP Files to glTF and the config.json format is at Custom Assets. Large .glb files slow AdvantageScope down. If one passes roughly 50 MB, simplify the model (no bolts, no small holes) and consider not versioning the .glb files (or using Git LFS).

Each moving part is registered once, with its model number and the point it rotates around. The template doesn't ship a visualizer, so add the registration to your own RobotContainer, for example in a configureVisualizer() method that the constructor calls: // model_0.glb: the intake, rotating around the pivot axis. RobotVisualizer.component( 0, MechanismPoses.pivot(IntakeConstants.PIVOT_AXIS, Axis.PITCH, intake::getPivotAngle), IntakeConstants.PIVOT_AXIS); PIVOT_AXIS: a point on the rotation axis, measured in the CAD in meters (X forward, Y to the left, Z up, from the center of the chassis on the ground). Axis.PITCH with a positive angle raises the front; Axis.YAW rotates counter-clockwise as seen from above (turrets). For elevators use MechanismPoses.slider(start, direction, subsystem::getHeight), and for a part mounted on another part (an arm on an elevator carriage) use MechanismPoses.attach(parent, child).

Run the simulation once (./gradlew simulateJava). It writes Robot_MyRobot/config.generated.json with one component per registered part, already carrying the zeroedPosition that brings each part's axis to the origin (that's how AdvantageScope expects a "zeroed" part). Copy the components list into config.json. The default rotations (x 90°, then z 90°) work for models exported from Onshape. If the robot shows up lying down or rotated, adjust rotations and zeroedRotations together.

In AdvantageScope, use App > Use Custom Assets Folder (on macOS the menu is called AdvantageScope) and pick this advantagescope/ folder, the one containing Robot_MyRobot. That way the model updates along with each git pull. Open a 3D Field tab, drag the robot's pose (RealOutputs/Subsystems/Drivetrain/Odometry/Pose) and pick the team's model (the name in config.json). Drag RealOutputs/Visualizer/Components onto the robot and pick Components. If a part rotates around the wrong point, PIVOT_AXIS doesn't match the CAD. If it rotates the wrong way, flip the sign of the angle the subsystem reports.

The whole robot is a conversation of requests between layers, each with its own state machine: Driver. SuperStructureCommands.manageRequests(...) is the SuperStructure's default command: it reads the buttons every cycle and writes a RobotRequest through a priority table (the first true row wins). SuperStructure. The overall state machine (SuperStructureBase) decides the robot's state. bindRequest(request, entryState, statesThatAlreadyServeIt...) says which state it enters to serve each request. In each overall state's onEnter, it sets each subsystem's request. Subsystems. Each one is a StateSubsystem<Request, State, Inputs, IO> with its own state machine (fsm.state(...), bindRequest(...)). atGoal() says whether the requested state has been reached, and the SuperStructure uses that in its transitions. Relay. Each subsystem's default command is generated by @AutoCommandFactory (XxxCommands.defaultCommand(superStructure, xxx)): it copies superStructure.getXxxRequest() into the subsystem every cycle. Co-driver. The manual backup: XxxCommands.<request>(xxx) overrides a subsystem's request while the button is held (override, which lasts one cycle and is renewed by the command). The SuperStructure's request is still stored and atGoal() is still relative to it, so the overall FSM never advances because of an override. Release the button, and the subsystem goes back to following the SuperStructure on its own. Hardware only through IO. A subsystem never talks to a motor directly: it calls io.controlXxx(), which returns a MotorController. In replay the IO is empty and inputs come from the log, so the same code runs on the robot, in simulation and in replay.

All in org.ciprix.interfaces.fsm.StateMachine: Feature Use transitionTo(target, condition) A local state transition transitionTo(target, condition, seconds) Only fires once the condition has held true for that long (debounce) waitFor(condition) / waitFor(seconds) Waits before moving to the next state timeoutAfter(seconds[, safetyState]) A state that takes too long falls back to the safety state transitionToSecurityState(condition) and addSecurityTransition(condition) Failure paths; the request that failed stays blocked until it's released, so the FSM doesn't return straight to the state that just failed regularTime(min, max) A state's normal duration, with per-state statistics in the log inState(...) A Trigger active in one or more states (LEDs, controller rumble) toMermaid() A diagram of the machine, also logged once

Ciprix holds what serves any team: FSM, StateSubsystem, motors with intent and health, physics simulation, vision, power management, self-test, 3D visualization and utilities. Each team's robot project holds what's theirs: the subsystems, the season's SuperStructure, shot tables, vision standard-deviation maps and button bindings. Rule of thumb: if another team would use it the same way, it belongs in the library; if it depends on the robot or the game, it stays in the robot project.
The step-by-step guide, with a compiling example, is in the skeleton.

Ciprix's motors remember the code's intent: A command only goes to the hardware when it changes, and is resent every 0.5 s. A state that repeats runVelocity(...) every cycle doesn't flood the CAN bus. A motor that never received a command (a follower, for example) is never touched. Automatic un-jam (withStallReversal(...)) reverses the motor briefly, then restores the last command the code actually requested. Health (connected, faults, stalled, free-spinning, temperature) comes through the inputs and the alerts. The same MotorConfig works for Talon FX, Talon FXS, SPARK MAX/Flex, Talon SRX/Victor SPX, PWM and the simulated motor.

Package org.ciprix.controller. Helpers to read the driver's input and give feedback. Class What it does NaturalXboxController A CommandXboxController with a deadband and inverted axes, so the values follow the robot frame (+X forward, +Y to the left): pushing a stick up or to the left gives a positive value, and pushing it down or to the right gives a negative one. The X axes are inverted on purpose. Also has squared variants for finer control near the center. ArcadeController A generic arcade stick with up to 16 buttons, each exposed as a Trigger (button1() to button16(), or button(index)). DoublePressTracker Turns any Trigger into one that fires only on a quick double press. VibrateXboxController Command factory for rumble patterns. UtilCalculus Converts the two joystick axes into a translation vector.

NaturalXboxController driver = new NaturalXboxController(0, 0.08); // port, deadband double forward = driver.getLeftY(); // up is positive (+X forward) double left = driver.getLeftX(); // left is positive (+Y left) double turn = driver.getSquaredRightX(); // same axis, squared Without the second argument, the deadband is CiprixSettings.getControllerDeadband(). Change it at runtime with setDeadband(...).

UtilCalculus.getLinearVelocityFromJoysticks(x, y) keeps the stick's direction and squares its magnitude, so small movements are gentle and full deflection is still full speed: Translation2d input = UtilCalculus.getLinearVelocityFromJoysticks( driver.getLeftY(), driver.getLeftX()); The result is in the driver frame described in Driving helpers.

Trigger reset = DoublePressTracker.doublePress(driver.start()); reset.onTrue(Commands.runOnce(drive::zeroHeading)); The second press has to start within DoublePressTracker.maxLengthSecs (0.4 s) of the first.

VibrateXboxController rumble = new VibrateXboxController(driver); driver.a().onTrue(rumble.lightConfirm()); intake.hasGamePiece().onTrue(rumble.pulses(0.8, 3, 0.6)); // intensity, pulses, total seconds Available patterns: continuous, pulses, zigZag, rampUp, lightConfirm and heavyWarning. Each one is a Command that stops the rumble when it ends or is interrupted.

AdvantageKit is the logging and replay framework created by Littleton Robotics, FRC Team 6328 "Mechanical Advantage". Ciprix is built around it: CiprixRobot configures AdvantageKit's Logger, the IO-layer pattern of the subsystems follows its recommended structure, and log replay and @AutoLogOutput come from it. Its official documentation is at docs.advantagekit.org. Origin: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit Copyright: © 2021–2026 Littleton Robotics. License: a BSD-style license (keep the copyright notice and disclaimer; don't use the names of Littleton Robotics, FRC 6328, AdvantageKit or its contributors to endorse derived products). It is not the MIT license. Read the LICENSE file for the exact terms; this page is a summary, not legal advice. How this affects your team: AdvantageKit is not embedded in Ciprix. Ciprix.json only declares it in the "requires" block, and WPILib's vendordep manager downloads it from its own repository, with its license. A few small utility classes are adapted from AdvantageKit's templates and from the 6328 robot code (SparkUtil, PhoenixUtil, SwitchableChooser, DoublePressTracker, LoggedTunableNumber, GeomUtil). They keep their original headers and are listed in the NOTICE file. The text and code of this documentation are original. Only the sidebar-style layout of the site is inspired by AdvantageKit's documentation. No logo, text or name of AdvantageKit is used as a brand here. Ciprix adapts to CTRE Phoenix, REVLib and PathPlanner. Each keeps its own license; install them from their official vendordeps. The pathfinding example used by LocalADStarAK comes from PathPlanner's author, Michael Jansen (PathPlanner is MIT licensed).
Built with Docusaurus (MIT) and the local search plugin (MIT).

Package org.ciprix.util.drivetrain. Small, composable pieces that sit between the driver's sticks and the drivetrain. The library never depends on your drivetrain class: your drive subsystem implements DriveContext and every helper works with it. public class Drive extends SubsystemBase implements DriveContext, DriveAccelerationLimits { @Override public Pose2d getPose() { ... } @Override public ChassisSpeeds getRobotVelocity() { ... } @Override public LinearVelocity getMaxSpeed() { ... } @Override public AngularVelocity getMaxAngularSpeed() { ... } // DriveAccelerationLimits is only needed for anti-tipping, see Safety. }

Translation modifiers work in the driver frame: the joystick vector normalized to [-1, 1], where +X points away from the driver's own alliance wall. It is the same on both alliances, so modifiers chain without caring about the color. Convert to field speeds once, at the end, with AllianceFlipUtil.apply(drivetrain, vx, vy, omega). That method expects m/s and rad/s, not the normalized values, so multiply the modifiers' output by drivetrain.getMaxSpeed() first (and the rotation output of a RotationStrategy, which is already in rad/s, goes in as omega unchanged). A modifier that computes a direction from field positions (a target, a zone center) must convert it first with TranslationModifier.fieldToDriver(...).

A TranslationModifier is one method: Translation2d apply(DriveContext, Translation2d input). Modifier Effect ThrottleMapModifier Non-linear stick curve (fine control at low speed). TargetAssistModifier(targetSupplier, weight) Blends the stick toward a field target. ZoneSuctionModifier(zone, strength) Inside the zone, pulls the robot through its center line and across it. ZoneRepulsionModifier(zone, strength) Pushes the robot away from a zone it should not enter. DualZoneSuctionBumpModifier(zoneA, zoneB, strength) Guides the robot from one zone to the other (crossing a bump, for example). Chain them in order: List<TranslationModifier> modifiers = List.of( new ThrottleMapModifier(), new ZoneRepulsionModifier(wallZone, 0.6), new TargetAssistModifier(() -> FieldPositions.hub(), 0.3)); Translation2d input = UtilCalculus.getLinearVelocityFromJoysticks(driver.getLeftY(), driver.getLeftX()); for (TranslationModifier m : modifiers) { input = m.apply(drive, input); } // `rotation` is any RotationStrategy (see below). Normalized [-1, 1] -> m/s, then driver frame -> field-relative speeds. double maxSpeed = drive.getMaxSpeed().in(MetersPerSecond); ChassisSpeeds speeds = AllianceFlipUtil.apply( drive, input.getX() * maxSpeed, input.getY() * maxSpeed, rotation.calculate(drive));

A RotationStrategy returns the angular velocity each cycle with calculate(DriveContext) and can be reset with reset(DriveContext) when you switch to it. Strategy Behavior ManualRotation(stick, maxSpeed) The driver's rotation stick. PIDRotation(targetSupplier[, manualControl]) Holds a heading with a PID. If a manual supplier is given, the stick takes over while it is outside the deadband. The output is limited to the drivetrain's max angular speed. HeadingStickRotation(xStick, yStick) Points the robot where the right stick points. The PID gains are shared by every PIDRotation and tunable under Drive/RotationPID. To start from your own gains call PIDRotation.setDefaultGains(kP, kI, kD) once, before creating the first instance.
DriveAccelerationLimits is the small interface the safety features use to change the drivetrain's acceleration limits at runtime. See Safety.
Three steps take a new WPILib project to a Ciprix robot: install the vendordep, copy the template and extend CiprixRobot.

In the WPILib VS Code extension, run WPILib: Manage Vendor Libraries → Install new library (online) and paste: https://23daniel3.github.io/Ciprix/Ciprix.json To pin a version, use https://23daniel3.github.io/Ciprix/vendordeps/<version>/Ciprix.json instead (for example 2026.3.0). Ciprix.json bundles every Ciprix module (core, CTRE Phoenix 6, Phoenix 5, REV, PathPlanner) and commons-math3. It also declares AdvantageKit and WPILibNewCommands in its "requires" block, so VS Code offers to install them if the project doesn't have them yet. Beyond that, install only the official vendordep for the hardware or path library your robot actually uses: Phoenix 6, Phoenix 5, REVLib or PathPlannerLib. Unused vendor integrations are never loaded at runtime. Then add the annotation processor, which generates each subsystem's XxxCommands, to build.gradle: def ciprixJson = new groovy.json.JsonSlurper().parseText(new File(projectDir.getAbsolutePath() + "/vendordeps/Ciprix.json").text) annotationProcessor "org.ciprix:ciprix-processor:$ciprixJson.version"

The fastest start is the templates/skeleton folder: the smallest complete robot in the pattern, with one subsystem (Roller), the SuperStructure, the driver commands and the co-driver backup. Copy the folder outside the Ciprix repository (or download it from GitHub). In .wpilib/wpilib_preferences.json, change teamNumber to your team's number. In settings.gradle, change rootProject.name. Open the folder in the WPILib VS Code extension. Simulate Robot Code already works: the simulated roller spins with the driver's left bumper (controller 0) and reverses with the right one. Outside the Ciprix repository, Gradle downloads the published version listed in vendordeps/Ciprix.json.

Robot extends CiprixRobot instead of LoggedRobot. The base class sets up AdvantageKit logging (USB and NetworkTables on the robot, NetworkTables in simulation, and log replay), the runtime and tuning modes, CiprixSettings, the default PreMatchChecklist and the CommandScheduler lifecycle. This is the skeleton's Robot.java: package frc.robot; import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Command; import org.ciprix.CiprixRobot; import org.ciprix.CiprixSettings; public class Robot extends CiprixRobot { private final RobotContainer robotContainer; public Robot() { super(Constants.simMode, Constants.tuningMode); robotContainer = new RobotContainer(); } @Override protected void configure() { CiprixSettings.setControllerDeadband(Constants.CONTROLLER_DEADBAND); CiprixSettings.setDefaultAlliance(Constants.DEFAULT_ALLIANCE); CiprixSettings.setFieldSize(Constants.FIELD_LENGTH_METERS, Constants.FIELD_WIDTH_METERS); } @Override protected Command getAutonomousCommand() { return robotContainer.getAutonomousCommand(); } } The lifecycle methods are final, so the scheduler can't be switched off by accident. Use the periodic(), autonomousStart(), teleopStart() and testStart() hooks, and adjust CiprixSettings in configure().

Read Architecture to see how requests and state machines fit together, and how to add a subsystem. Run the robot in Simulation before touching hardware. Coming from 2026.2.x? See the migration steps in the Release notes.

Every motor the code reads (and every camera in AprilTagVision) feeds into HardwareHealthMonitor, which publishes: Key (/AdvantageKit/RealOutputs/...) What it is Hardware/Blink Toggles at 2.5 Hz while something is wrong; stays false once everything is fine Hardware/Healthy True when everything is connected, with no faults and no problems Hardware/Disconnected Names of the devices that aren't responding Hardware/Problems One line per fault or problem, like Intake/Roller: Over temperature To make the driver's screen flash red: in Elastic, a Boolean Box bound to Hardware/Blink, red for true and the background color for false. Next to it, a list showing Hardware/Problems says what it is. HardwareHealthMonitor.blink() also works for an LED effect. Motors the code never reads (followers, for example) aren't judged, and nothing counts as disconnected during the first 5 s after power-on.

documents.t: new MotorConfig().withStallReversal(Amps.of(30), 0.2, 0.3, 0.5) If the motor is being commanded, draws over 30 A and barely turns for 0.2 s, it reverses at 50% for 0.3 s and then returns on its own to the last command the code actually requested. While it reverses, the code's commands are kept, not dropped; a stop() still stops it immediately. inputs.stalled and inputs.unjamming show up in the log.

PowerManager watches the filtered battery voltage and, below 9.5 V, lowers the current limit of NORMAL and LOW priority motors and smooths the drivetrain's acceleration; below 8 V it cuts further. It steps back up one level at a time once the battery stays 0.5 V above the threshold for 0.5 s. Priority Normal Below 9.5 V Below 8 V HIGH (default) 100% 100% 100% NORMAL 100% 75% 50% LOW 100% 50% 25% new MotorConfig().currentLimit(Amps.of(35)).powerPriority(PowerPriority.LOW) A common setup: rollers and conveyors as LOW, and match-deciding mechanisms (shooter, drivetrain) without reduction (the drivetrain only gets smoother acceleration). In the log: Power/Level and Power/FilteredVoltage.

Each subsystem declares, alongside its state machine, which motors can spin freely for a moment: selfTest() .motor("Roller", io::controlRollerMotor, () -> inputs.rollerMotorInputs) .output(0.3) .currentBetween(Amps.of(0.3), Amps.of(25)) .mustTurn(RotationsPerSecond.of(5)); With the robot enabled, the SelfTest/<subsystem> and SelfTest/All dashboard buttons spin each motor and check that it responds, draws a reasonable current and actually turns. It catches a disconnected motor or wire, a broken coupling, a dead encoder and a jammed mechanism. During the test the subsystem's state machine is paused and, at the end, restarts from its initial state. The result shows up at SelfTest/<subsystem>/<motor> and a failure becomes an alert. Don't use it on an arm or elevator, which would hit its hard stop.

With the robot disabled, PreMatchChecklist shows what's still missing before the match: PreMatchChecklist.addDefaults(); // battery >= 12.4 V, devices connected, no faults PreMatchChecklist.add("Alliance set", () -> DriverStation.getAlliance().isPresent()); PreMatchChecklist.add("Vision located the robot", vision::hasRecentPose); In Elastic: a Boolean Box on PreMatch/Ready and a list on PreMatch/Pending. A warning alert lists what's pending. Once the robot is enabled, the checklist stops and the alert disappears.
Based on the official 2027 changelog, still in alpha (Alpha 8, page updated 2026-10-30). Before migrating, check the final version at New for 2027 and Removed features.

The pattern doesn't change: the driver writes requests, the SuperStructure decides the robot's state, each subsystem has its own state machine, the co-driver overrides a subsystem while holding a button, and hardware is only ever reached through IO. Ciprix's state machine doesn't depend on the command scheduler, and StateSubsystem is still a command-based "v2" SubsystemBase, which keeps existing in 2027. This migration is about names and APIs, not architecture.

Change Where it shows up here roboRIO replaced by the Systemcore, with several CAN buses CAN devices start taking a CANPort; the CTRE and REV IOs follow whatever the vendors ship for 2027 Java 25 and Gradle 9.4.1 sourceCompatibility in Ciprix's build.gradle and in each project's build.gradle edu.wpi.first packages become org.wpilib Every file; the VS Code importer tries to rename them automatically DriverStation split into MatchState and RobotState Our Constants.RobotState now shares a name with a WPILib class: rename it to SuperState during migration (RobotContainer imports wpilibj.*) SmartDashboard, SendableChooser and Sendable replaced by Telemetry and Tunables; Shuffleboard removed SelfTest/... buttons, LoggedDashboardChooser (depends on AdvantageKit 2027), PersistentAlert Timestamps are integer nanoseconds VisionIOLimelight (getFPGATime() and NetworkTables timestamps, in microseconds) Rotation2d.getDegrees()/getRadians() return the "wrapped" angle Check any math that relies on a continuous angle (there's a ContinuousUnwrapper for this) MathUtil.clamp is gone, use Math.clamp; Pose.exp(twist) becomes plus(twist.exp()) 6 library files (acceleration limiters, anti-tipping, ThrottleMap, SimMechanism) and the robot's Drivetrain MotorController.set() becomes setThrottle(); PWM controllers move to a drivers library The library's PWM IOs (interfaces/motor/pwm) AprilTag and CameraServer become vendordeps; AprilTagFields moves into a Fields class VisionConstants and the VisionFilter.field(...) example Jackson replaced by Avaje Jsonb The robot's LimelightHelpers uses Jackson: swap it for the 2027 version of the file, or for the library's VisionIOLimelight, which doesn't need it Test mode becomes Utility; robotInit() is gone (we already use the constructor) Robot.java Counters, servo, SPI, analog gyros and other devices leave the Systemcore Nothing here uses them

documents.t: 2027 brings a new command-based framework ("v3") with a declarative state machine and a Mechanism interface, documented alongside v2. For the 2027 season, the safe path is to stay on v2. In the offseason, it's worth evaluating a StateSubsystem built on top of a v3 Mechanism with the same API (fsm, bindRequest, override, selfTest), so the robot code doesn't need to change at all.

A wpilib-2027 branch, with the WPILib 2027 VS Code extension. core first: switch the GradleRIO version, let the importer rename the packages, update the table above and run the tests (most run without the HAL). ctre, rev and phoenix5 once CTRE and REV publish their 2027 releases (Phoenix 5 may not have a Systemcore version). templates/skeleton, which is small and quickly shows what's still missing. Each team's robot: rename RobotState to SuperState, swap LimelightHelpers, check the whole simulation and replay a 2026 log. Only then power it up on the Systemcore, with the robot suspended.
Versions follow <season>.<minor>.<patch>. Every release is on GitHub, where the full changelog lives.
The final Ciprix release for the 2026 season. Setup is simpler: one vendordep and one base class. It also adds more than 40 test classes and fixes the bugs those tests found.

CiprixRobot. Robot extends CiprixRobot instead of LoggedRobot. It sets up AdvantageKit logging, the runtime and tuning modes, AutoLogOutputManager, the default pre-match checklist and the command scheduler. See Getting started. One vendordep. Ciprix.json bundles every module and commons-math3. New guides: Controllers, Zones, Driving helpers, Safety and Tunables and dashboard.

Vendordeps. Update Ciprix.json, then delete vendordeps/Ciprix-CTRE.json, Ciprix-REV.json, Ciprix-Phoenix5.json and Ciprix-PathPlanner.json. You can also remove the commons-math3 line from build.gradle. Robot.java. Extend CiprixRobot: call super(Constants.simMode, Constants.tuningMode), move the CiprixSettings.set... calls into configure(), return your auto from getAutonomousCommand(), and remove your own Logger setup and scheduler calls. Use CiprixSettings.Mode instead of your own Mode enum. LoggedRobot still works if you are not ready to switch. Behavior changes. Retest these on the robot: ShotOnTheMoveCalculator: the sign of the lateral compensation angle is fixed. Remove any workaround that flipped it. AntiTipping / AntiTippingAccel: the correction is now robot-relative (+pitch drives +X, +roll drives −Y). TargetAssistModifier, ZoneRepulsionModifier, DualZoneSuctionBumpModifier: they now convert field directions to the driver frame. Before, they pushed the wrong way on Red. AllianceSelector.isRed() / isBlue() use the resolved alliance, matching AllianceFlipUtil. PIDRotation: the output is limited to the drivetrain's max angular speed.

TunableControls: the copy constructor keeps the profiled flag, plain controllers apply the period, velocity tolerance and continuous input, and tunable controllers read their gains as soon as they are created. AntiTippingAccel reads the nominal limits once and restores them correctly; reset() clears all state; new getLastState() for logging. SuperStructureBase rejects a null initial request before the subsystem is registered. REV: SPARKs no longer print the REVLib "kG is overriden by kCos" warning on every boot.

TranslationModifier.fieldToDriver(...) for custom modifiers. EncoderIOCANcoder(name, id, CANBus, config) and getCANcoder(). MotorIOTalonSRX.getTalon() and MotorIOVictorSPX.getVictor(). PreMatchChecklist.addDefaults() can be called more than once safely.

Pure-logic tests (filters, zones, slew limiters, detectors, alliance flip, drivetrain assists, anti-tipping, encoders, SuperStructure, motors, tunables, shot calculator, controllers) and hardware tests on the vendor simulators (Phoenix 6, REVLib, Phoenix 5 and every PWM motor type).
Documentation release: all guides and code comments were translated to English.

First release of Ciprix as a library, published as a vendordep: the core, CTRE, REV, Phoenix 5, PathPlanner and annotation-processor modules, with a Maven repository and Ciprix*.json files on GitHub Pages, plus the robot template in templates/skeleton.
Package org.ciprix.util.security. Protections that keep the robot and its mechanisms alive. For hardware alerts and the pit checklist, see Hardware, power and pit.

DynamicSlewRateLimiter limits how fast a velocity can change, like WPILib's SlewRateLimiter, but the acceleration limits can change every cycle and the API uses WPILib units. DynamicSlewRateLimiter limiter = new DynamicSlewRateLimiter(MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(6.0)); LinearVelocity vx = limiter.calculate(MetersPerSecond.of(requestedVx)); // Asymmetric limits (accelerate and decelerate differently), changeable at any time: limiter.setAccelerationLimits(MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(6.0), MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(9.0)); limiter.reset(MetersPerSecond.of(0.0)); AngularDynamicSlewRateLimiter is the same for angular velocity.

Both detectors are BooleanSuppliers and can also become a Trigger with asTrigger(). // True when the current stays above 60 A for 0.25 s. CurrentSpikeDetector spike = new CurrentSpikeDetector(60.0, 0.25); boolean tripped = spike.update(motorInputs.current.in(Amps)); // True when the motor should be moving but is below 0.5 rot/s for 0.3 s. // Never trips while the robot is disabled. LockedMotorDetector locked = new LockedMotorDetector(0.3, 0.5); locked.update(commandedSpeed != 0, motorInputs.velocity.in(RotationsPerSecond)); Call update(...) once per cycle.

Two options. Both need the IMU's rotation, and both return Optional<ChassisSpeeds> with a correction to add to the driver's speeds when the robot is tipping. AntiTipping(kP, thresholdDegrees, maxCorrectionSpeed): proportional correction toward the low side of the tilt, robot-relative (a positive pitch drives +X, a positive roll drives -Y). AntiTippingAccel(config): also estimates risk from the IMU's acceleration and your robot's center of mass, and lowers the drivetrain's acceleration limits before the tip happens. Your drivetrain must implement DriveContext and DriveAccelerationLimits. Tune it through AntiTippingAccel.AntiTippingConfig (center of mass height and offsets, thresholds, weights). getLastState() returns a record that is ready to log. AntiTippingAccel antiTip = new AntiTippingAccel(new AntiTippingAccel.AntiTippingConfig()); Optional<ChassisSpeeds> fix = antiTip.calculate( imu.getRotation3d(), MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(imu.getAccelX()), // your IMU's reading, converted to units MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(imu.getAccelY()), drive); // addCorrection is a method of your own drivetrain, not of the library: add the speeds // to the driver's request however your drive code does it. fix.ifPresent(speeds -> drive.addCorrection(speeds)); Call reset() when the robot is re-enabled so the limits and smoothing start clean.

CANHealthMonitor takes the devices in the physical order of the CAN chain and logs the most likely failure point (before the first device, or between two devices) when one stops answering. CANHealthMonitor can = new CANHealthMonitor("rio", new CANHealthMonitor.CANDeviceStatus("Gyro", 1, imu::isConnected), new CANHealthMonitor.CANDeviceStatus("FL Drive", 2, flDrive::isConnected)); // robotPeriodic: can.checkHealth();

Simulation uses the same configuration and motor names as the robot, so state machines, gains, alerts and logs behave the same way. Simulate Robot Code in VS Code (or ./gradlew simulateJava) opens the simulation; enable the robot in the simulation window.

MotorIOSim mimics the real controller (velocity/position loop, Motion Magic/Smart Motion, kS/kV/kA/kG, current limit, un-jam, health) on top of a physical model of the mechanism: private final MotorIOSim flywheel = MotorIOSim.talonFX( "Shooter/Leader", ShooterConstants.MOTOR_LEADER_CONFIG, SimMechanism.flywheel(DCMotor.getKrakenX60(2), 1.0, 0.004).withFriction(0.03, 0.0)) .withFollowers(1); Mechanism Factory Roller, conveyor SimMechanism.roller(motor, reduction, inertia) Flywheel SimMechanism.flywheel(motor, reduction, inertia) Arm, pivot SimMechanism.arm(motor, reduction, massKg, lengthM), with gravity Elevator SimMechanism.elevator(motor, reduction, massKg, drumRadiusM), with gravity Adjustments: withFriction(coulombNm, viscous), withLimits(minRot, maxRot) (hard stops), withStartPosition(rot), withGravity(...) and withLoad(...) (an attached piece, for example). MotorIOSim.talonFX(...) uses Talon units and gains; MotorIOSim.spark(...) uses SPARK's (kV in V/RPM, as in the REV Hardware Client). To test how the robot reacts to problems: setConnected(false), setFaults("...") and setTemperatureCelsius(95) trigger the same alerts as the real robot.
Every simulated motor adds its current draw to SimBattery, which sags the voltage like a real battery. That's what makes power management kick in during simulation too.

With Constants.simMode = Mode.REPLAY, the robot re-runs an AdvantageKit log: the IOs are empty and inputs come from the log. This is useful for testing a logic change (a vision filter, an FSM transition) against the data from a real match, and comparing it in AdvantageScope.
The CAD's moving parts follow the mechanisms (RobotVisualizer and MechanismPoses). The step-by-step guide is in 3D Robot.

core/src/test has the library's tests. Most run without the HAL, with TestEnvironment controlling the clock, the enabled state and the battery. It's the fastest way to prove a new rule works before taking it to the robot.
Package org.ciprix.logger. Values you can change from the dashboard while testing, and choosers for the autonomous selector.

LoggedTunableNumber returns its default value in a match and the dashboard's value in tuning mode (CiprixSettings.isTuningMode(), read on every call). Outside tuning mode no NetworkTables entry is created and hasChanged(...) is always false, so it costs nothing. private final LoggedTunableNumber kP = new LoggedTunableNumber("Arm/kP", 4.0); @Override public void periodic() { // Apply only when a value actually changed. The id must be unique per consumer. LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged(hashCode(), () -> motor.setPID(kP.get(), 0, 0), kP); } LoggedTunableUnit is the same for WPILib units; the key gets the unit symbol appended ("Flywheel/CurrentLimit (A)"): LoggedTunableUnit limit = new LoggedTunableUnit("Flywheel/CurrentLimit", Amps.of(40)); Current c = limit.get(); Motors already expose their PID, feedforward and motion profile to the dashboard through the motor classes, so most subsystems never need to create tunables by hand.

SwitchableChooser is a string chooser whose options can change while the robot is running: SwitchableChooser startPosition = new SwitchableChooser("Auto/Start"); startPosition.setOptions(new String[] {"Left", "Center", "Right"}); String chosen = startPosition.get(); LoggedSequentialDashboardChooser<V> is a chain of N choosers, one per step of an autonomous routine, where each slot can filter the options of the next (for example, only the scoring spots reachable from the chosen start). Call periodic() from robotPeriodic(). var chooser = new LoggedSequentialDashboardChooser<Supplier<Command>>("Auto/Step", 3); chooser.addDefaultOption("None", Commands::none); chooser.addOption("Score A", () -> autos.scoreA()); chooser.setFilter(1, key -> !key.equals("Score A")); // slot 1 can't repeat A List<Supplier<Command>> steps = chooser.get();
Vision has two levels: the library's ready-made pipeline, which works for any team, and the extra rules each team can add on their own robot.

Works with Limelight without needing LimelightHelpers: vision = new AprilTagVision( drivetrain::addVisionMeasurement, drivetrain::getPose, () -> drivetrain.getState().Speeds) .withCamera("Front", new VisionIOLimelight("limelight-front", drivetrain::getRotation)) .withCamera("Back", new VisionIOLimelight("limelight-back", drivetrain::getRotation), 1.5) .withFilter( new VisionFilter() .field(AprilTagFieldLayout.loadField(AprilTagFields.k2026RebuiltWelded)) .maxDistance(4.0)); VisionIOLimelight reads every new frame from the NetworkTables queue, so none is lost and none is used twice, and delivers both MegaTag 1 and MegaTag 2 poses. VisionFilter rejects, with a reason: pose outside the field, robot off the ground or tilted, tags too far away, an ambiguous single tag (MegaTag 1), too fast a turn for MegaTag 2, and, if enabled with maxJump(meters), a single tag "jumping" far from the current estimate while it's still trusted. After 1 s with no accepted pose the estimate stops being trusted and the robot re-finds itself. VisionStdDevs computes the standard deviation as distance² divided by the number of tags. On MegaTag 2 the angle comes from the gyro itself, so the angle's standard deviation is ignored. The number passed to withCamera (1.5 above) multiplies the deviations of a less trustworthy camera. In the log, each camera has Vision/<camera>/AcceptedPoses, RejectedPoses, LastRejection, AcceptedCount, RejectedCount and TagPoses, and a camera that stops responding shows up in the hardware alerts. In replay, use new VisionIO() {} for each camera.

When a team needs a tighter filter, keep a Vision subsystem in the robot project with the team's own maps (distance, velocity, ambiguity) and add the library's rules on top. Rules that tend to be worth it: Judge each frame once. If you read the Limelight as a "last value" every cycle, the same frame enters the estimator across several cycles and the estimator trusts it too much. Season field bounds, robot on the ground, fast turns, and single-tag jumps (maxJump(meters)). Trust MegaTag 1's angle only with 2 or more tags. Otherwise use the gyro's angle and ignore the angle's standard deviation: correcting the gyro with itself only injects the camera's latency. Log the reason for each rejection (for example Vision/<CAMERA>/RejectReason). To tune: look at the rejection reasons and the poses in AdvantageScope after a practice run. If a rule rejects too many good frames, loosen its constant.
Use the layout for the event's field: AprilTagFields.k2026RebuiltAndymark or AprilTagFields.k2026RebuiltWelded. The filter's bounds come from that layout.

Package org.ciprix.zones. Areas of the field defined in code, used to assist the driver, slow the robot down or choose a behavior from where the robot is. Class Shape Rectangle2d Axis-aligned rectangle from two opposite corners. Circle2d Center (fixed or supplied each cycle, for a moving target) and radius. Polygon2d Any polygon, clockwise or not, including self-intersecting ones (even-odd rule). Zone2d<Z> Pairs any of the above with an enum constant so you can ask "which zone am I in?". All shapes implement ZoneIO: contains(point), distanceTo(point) and getCenter(). Coordinates follow the WPILib field frame (origin at the Blue Alliance corner). Rectangle2d trench = new Rectangle2d(new Translation2d(4.0, 0.0), new Translation2d(5.5, 1.3)); Circle2d hub = new Circle2d(new Translation2d(4.6, 4.0), 1.2); boolean inTrench = trench.contains(drive.getPose().getTranslation()); double toHub = hub.distanceTo(drive.getPose().getTranslation()); // meters

enum FieldZone { TRENCH, HUB } List<Zone2d<FieldZone>> zones = List.of( new Zone2d<>(FieldZone.TRENCH, trench), new Zone2d<>(FieldZone.HUB, hub)); Optional<FieldZone> where = zones.stream() .filter(z -> z.contains(pose.getTranslation())) .map(Zone2d::getId) .findFirst();

Define zones once for the Blue Alliance and mirror them when you are on Red with AllianceFlipUtil.apply(polygon, flipX, flipY, useAllianceColor), the same way you mirror poses with AllianceFlipUtil.apply(pose). Pass true for the axes to mirror (usually both for a rotationally symmetric field, or only X for a mirrored one) and true for useAllianceColor so it only flips on Red.
ZoneSuctionModifier, ZoneRepulsionModifier and DualZoneSuctionBumpModifier take Polygon2d zones and change the driver's translation input. See Driving helpers.
